**Russian gas flows via Ukraine for last day as transit deal crumbles | Euractiv**
Russian gas flows through Ukraine are set to cease from the early hours of 1 January, after Kyiv rejected a new transit agreement, marking the end of a five‑year deal that had allowed Russia to supply about 15 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas to Europe in 2023 – only 8 % of the 35 % peak share the Soviet Union once held in the European market. The loss of this route has already pushed gas prices to an all‑time high and contributed to inflation across the continent. President Vladimir Putin said last week that there was no time left this year to sign a new Ukrainian gas transit deal, blaming Kyiv for refusing to extend the agreement. Gazprom reported a net loss of $7 billion in 2023, its first annual loss since 1999, largely due to the loss of EU gas markets. The only remaining Russian pipelines to Europe are Blue Stream and TurkStream to Turkey; other routes such as Yamal‑Europe and Nord Stream are closed. Moldovan Prime Minister Dorin Recean ordered preparations for the possible nationalisation of Moldovagaz, which is 50 % owned by Gazprom, after the company announced it would suspend exports to Moldova from 0500 GMT on 1 January because of unpaid debts. Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico said Slovakia would consider reciprocal measures against Ukraine if the gas transit stops, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Fico of opening a ‘second energy front’ against Ukraine on the orders of Russia. Gazprom plans to send 42.4 million cubic metres of gas to Europe via Ukraine on Monday, a volume in line with recent days, but it assumes no further gas will flow after 31 December in its 2025 internal planning.

The facility remained operational and there were 'no casualties', and the drones caused 'minor damage' to a gas metering station, which emergency teams repaired quickly. TurkStream, which carries Russian gas to Turkey and Europe via Bulgaria, is one of Russia's last remaining pipeline routes after Ukraine refused to renew a five‑year transit deal earlier this year. The incident follows earlier reports of Ukrainian involvement in attacks on other Russian pipeline infrastructure, including the 2022 explosions on Nord Stream 1 and 2, for which the CIA allegedly warned Belgian authorities. Reuters could not independently confirm the incident, and Ukraine has not commented.

summary: Experts broadly agree that while the historical base rate for unexpected outages on major pipelines like TurkStream and Blue Stream is low, recent developments have substantially elevated the risk. Forecasters with technical, operational, geopolitical, and economic perspectives all cite the following risk-elevating factors: the intensifying Ukrainian campaign of drone and sabotage attacks on Russian energy infrastructure (including explicit attempts on TurkStream), the unique exposure of TurkStream as the last Russian gas export pipeline to Europe after Ukrainian transit ceased, and the broader escalation of hostilities. Attacks on comparable oil infrastructure have successfully caused temporary, unscheduled outages, and at least two attempted attacks on TurkStream’s Russian-side infrastructure have been reported in 2025. On the opposing side, experts highlight strong mitigating factors: the engineering resilience of both pipelines (especially offshore sections), rapid response and repair capabilities of Russian and Turkish operators, robust physical security, and the political and economic incentives for both Russia and Turkey to avoid disruption—especially as any outage could severely impact revenues and Turkey’s energy stability. The experts note that a 'Yes' outcome (unexpected cessation) requires only a brief, credibly reported halt unrelated to planned maintenance or contract changes. Probabilities assigned range mostly between 23% and 42%, with a consensus clustering around 28–38% (mean ≈ 33%), reflecting an acknowledgment of an unusually high-risk environment but ultimately greater confidence in the pipelines’ resilience and the strong mutual incentives of the stakeholders to prevent or quickly resolve disruptions. No scenario dominates, but the most likely outcome is continued operations without a confirmed unscheduled outage before January 1, 2026, though several forecasters warn that even a short, successful attack or technical incident could flip the outcome to 'Yes'.
